articles.title: British man arrested over suspected RAF Fairford terrorism plot
articles.summary:
Counter-terrorism policing says 22-year-old detained in London on suspicion of terrorism offences

A seventh man has been arrested in London on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of the…
articles.byline: Jamie Grierson Dan Sabbagh and Vikram Dodd

blocks.text: A seventh man has been arrested in London on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of the investigation related to threats to RAF Fairford, police have said.
The 22-year-old British national was arrested in Westminster, central London, on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, counter-terrorism policing said.

Police are continuing to investigate a so far unexplained incident on 27 September, when five men from London driving three white vans were arrested in the small hours in a village outside the Gloucestershire airbase used by bombers from the US air force.

A week later, on Sunday, the US decided to hastily withdraw all 12 of the B-1 Lancer bombers that had been based at Fairford back to the US. Some had only arrived at the base a week earlier, and refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled in order to complete the evacuation.

There remains speculation that Iran wants to target the base, which was used for US bombing runs on the country earlier this year, but the US and UK appear to have divergent views about the security situation and level of threat.

UK sources question whether Iran would have the capability to launch a Ukraine-style drone attack on military aircraft at the base, given the complexity of such an operation. On Monday, Downing Street said the base was safe.

But some reports suggested the US feared a drone strike along the lines of Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb attack on Russian airbases last year, and so did not want to leave its bombers stationed at Fairford.

On Monday night Donald Trump, the US president, said the aircraft had been moved because “there were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there?”

blocks.caption: Munitions sit beside the runway as a Rockwell B-1 Lancer heavy bomber departs from RAF Fairford on Sunday. Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: So far there has been no breakthrough in the investigation by counter-terror police. The five men detained in Whelford on 27 September were released on police bail a day later, without charge.
No explosive devices were found in their vans, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. One of the five had also called 999, and their intentions remain publicly unexplained.
On Thursday, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in Westminster on suspicion of terrorism offences. He was also released on bail on Saturday.

Speaking on Tuesday, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, Vicki Evans, said: “This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford.
“Once again, I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this highly complex investigation.

“We’re acutely aware of the public interest in this investigation, and we are working around the clock, and at pace, to identify the motivation behind events in Gloucestershire. We remain committed to investigating all possible angles.”
The 22-year-old is being held under rules that allow detectives to bail him, just like the other six men who have been arrested on a terrorism charge.

People arrested for terrorism offences can be held under two legal schedules which dictate how long they can be detained without charge. Under the terrorism schedule a suspect can be held for up to 14 days, but cannot be bailed, meaning police have a fortnight to charge or release them.

The 22-year-old arrested for alleged preparatory acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, a spokesperson for counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday. That means he could be released under investigation on bail, but detectives have much less time to hold him.
The five men arrested close to RAF Fairford were held under the same act before being bailed the next day, to the surprise of some.

Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days.
Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.
The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.
Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.

Counter-terrorism policing last week defended the move. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers,” Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police said.

articles.title: Whistleblower suit alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
articles.summary: The White House denies the allegations as ‘false’ and says the ‘first amendment does not protect violent rioting’

blocks.text: Donald Trump ordered the FBI to investigate protesters in Los Angeles who were demonstrating against the president’s immigration crackdown, according to a whistleblower complaint.

US senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat who represents California and serves on the Senate judiciary committee, said his office had received a copy of the complaint, which makes sweeping allegations about the Trump administration’s response to protests in LA in early 2025.
Demonstrators had been protesting against Trump’s deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to push the president’s agenda.

“These allegations are deeply alarming,” Padilla, who also serves as the top Democrat on the border security and immigration subcommittee, said in a statement. “Using the FBI to target Americans for exercising their first amendment rights directly undermines our nation’s foundational values. I won’t rest until we get answers.”

NBC first reported on the allegations after viewing a copy of the disclosure, which identifies the whistleblower as Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, who made the complaint following the federal response to anti-ICE protests around the city’s federal buildings, and in residential area, in February last year.

Fields alleges that Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told Akil Davis, the head of the field office to open an investigation into protesters’ activities outside federal buildings, even though Fields says the demonstrations were protected free speech, and several FBI employees in the field office expressed concern with the legality of these requests.

Field, who joined the FBI in May 2016, also alleges that Trump reportedly viewed a TikTok video of protesters in Alhambra, California that alerted neighbors about the presence of federal immigration officers and advised them of their legal rights. The White House, Fields says, then instructed Patel to direct the Los Angeles field office to initiate an investigation into those demonstrating in the video, because the president “was angry about the incident”.

Despite the fact that member of Fields’ team determined that the protesters’ actions were constitutionally protected and there was insufficient evidence, Fields was told by a colleague – whose name is redacted – that “the president wants this investigation”. Fields says that even though her supervisor acknowledged the investigation was unconstitutional, the directive still had to be followed.

Fields alleges that a “dedicated immigration squad” was created, comprising 10 agents, some of whom were taken off active cartel cases to carry out the White House’s requests. Fields says that she questioned the directives “operational logic” but her supervisor – whose name is also redacted in the complaint – described the move as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president”.

Fields says, however, she was not aware of any “actual or potential national security threat, federal criminal activity, or vulnerability” that would have warranted conducting assessments or opening investigations into anti-ICE and CBP protesters at the time.

She ultimately resigned from the bureau last year after she was removed from overseeing several programs, and believes that her diminished role was the result of objecting to protest-related investigations, according to the complaint.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called the allegations, laid out in the disclosure, “false” in a statement to the Guardian. “The first amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” she said. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
The FBI and justice department did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
In a letter to Todd Blanche, the attorney general, and Patel,

Padilla asks dozens of questions about the reported investigations, including whether they resulted in arrests, how many directives of this kind the justice department has received from the president and how many investigations are still open.

articles.title: Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
articles.summary: Crowds of mainly teenagers called for more resources for schools and an end to what they called police repression.
articles.byline: Paul Kirby, Hugh Schofield, Nick Beake, Mark Lowen

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions.
Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police.
Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers.
The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycées - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day.
Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement.
In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction.
A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed.
"Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart."

Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added.
There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases.

One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability".

Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the Château d'Épluches lycée for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone.
On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens.
Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired.
The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.

What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too.
Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September.

Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing.

"We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling.
Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris.

articles.title: Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns
articles.summary:
Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out the necessary environmental impact assessments

Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in…

blocks.text: Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in Finland after failing to do the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites.

The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajanni are part of a 13bn euro project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure.
It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representing Google, had felled 330-hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment.
In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land.
The Finnish Union for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres.

On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation.

The environmental impact assessment (EIA) is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said.

Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.”
after newsletter promotion
If Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine.
In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and admitted that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”.

The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.”

Tapani Veistola, chief operating officer at the Finnish Union for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appears to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, is “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.”
One of the reasons behind it, he said, is the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities.
“The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.”

articles.title: EU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members
articles.summary: The European Commission has put forward ideas it hopes will both ease the EU expansion process and allay concerns among existing members. Several countries, not least war-torn Ukraine, are among the…

image.caption: Expansion was a key issue at 'Berlin Process' talks in candidate country Montenegro this month seeking to further Western Balkan integration into the EUImage: Regierung von Montenegro

blocks.text: The European Commission on Tuesday published a document called "Preparing for a wider Union," which sought to lay out new proposals on "the policy orientations and actions needed to prepare the [European] Union for future enlargements."

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europe's future depends on the choices we make today," as she tries to encourage progress at the EU's leaders' summit this month and in other upcoming talks on the matter.

The EU's executive proposed an array of changes — including a gradual integration process for would-be members, new safeguards "to ensure that commitments undertaken during accession negotiations continue to be fulfiled steadily after accession," and changes to voting rules.

They were trying to strike a balance between simplifying the accession process, incentivizing candidate countries to continue to pursue it, and allaying concerns among existing members about potential risks or costs of expansion.

blocks.caption: Ukraine is the newest EU candidate country, seeking to accelerate the process amid Russia's invasionImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Why is expansion coming back into focus?
In the quarter century after the end of the Cold War, the EU rapidly grew from a union of 12 member states to 28, before dipping back down to 27 when the UK left following 2016's Brexit referendum.
But the process has ground to a halt ever since, with a series of candidate countries stuck in lengthy negotiations and little apparent appetite among members to continue to expand.

In recent years, amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine and signs of the US vying for increased influence in parts of Europe, theoretical interest in expansion has picked up once more. But realizing the idea, with strict rules governing the accession process and the need for unanimous support among existing members for many core steps, has remained challenging.
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028
What did the Commission say about expansion?
Von der Leyen said the Commission was trying to prepare institutions, adapt policies and adjust budgets to reflect shared realities to better facilitate and accommodate expansion.

"Enlargement of our Union is a geopolitical imperative," she said. "Today, we are laying the groundwork to ensure that a larger Union is also a stronger one: more resilient, more effective, and firmly anchored in the values and rules that define us."
She said that as countries progress on their path towards reform, "the EU must be ready to welcome them."

Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that Brussels' assessment "shows that the EU can accommodate a larger membership." But "there are areas where we see challenges we need to address," she acknowledged.
"One is the rule of law and sincere cooperation, where we are proposing stronger possibilities to prevent backsliding, including reducing funding or restricting voting rights," Kos said.
Why the US-EU rift is spilling into the Balkans
What changes are the European Commission proposing?
The Commission lays out a number of proposed changes or policies designed to smooth the accession process, including but not limited to:

items: Moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting among members in a number of the less significant votes about advancing or progressing membership bids
It makes no mention of changing the current requirement for a unanimous vote about finalizing membership applications, however
Gradual and accelerated integration of candidate countries to "bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses," but which would remain "conditional and reversible"

"Stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitements undertaken during the acession negotiations" in future accession treaties, which could "in the most serious cases" extend to the suspension of voting rights
Introducing "targeted arrangements" to "significantly limit financial support and market access" for sensitive agricultural products from candidate country Ukraine

Ukraine's vast agricultural sector had prompted some concerns among EU members looking at how the bloc's budget could handle expansion, given that agriculture is a rare policy area where the bulk of spending and subsidies are orchestrated at the EU level, not by national governments

blocks.text: All these proposals will be subject to further discussion among European leaders and governments, with the next major meeting being next week's EU leaders' summit. Should they gain traction and progress, no doubt after some alterations and amendments along the way, they would ultimately have to face and pass various voting procedures to be implemented.

blocks.caption: Moldova's President Maia Sandu is also a staunch advocate of her country joining the EUImage: Vladislav Culiomza/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's the current situation with EU candidate countries?
A total of eight countries currently have formal candidate status, meaning they are seeking to join the EU and have at least begun the often lengthy process that involves.

Some hope to join the bloc sooner rather than later, not least frontrunner Montenegro, after years of negotiations. Kos told DW last week that Montenegro was currently on track to become the next EU member by 2028.
Others, like Turkey, have nominally been candidates for decades but have made no discernible progress for years.

Ukraine is the newest addition to the list, having only gained full candidate status in 2024, but it is also the one with the most pressing motivation to hurry the process along amid Russia's invasion.
Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, North Macedonia and Serbia are also all seeking membership.
A ninth country, Kosovo, is recognized as a potential candidate but not a formal one — with not all EU members recognizing Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.

articles.title: Badenoch denies ‘British Iron Dome’ plan – after Tories use phrase in press release
articles.summary: Tory leader says proposed ‘Britannia Shield’ would not be comparable to Israeli missile defence system

blocks.text: Kemi Badenoch has denied she compared a new air defence system proposed by the party to Israel’s Iron Dome, despite using the term in her press release and a newspaper article.
The Conservative leader said the party’s proposed “Britannia Shield” would not be comparable to the missile defence system in Israel, which is primarily designed to counter short-range attacks.

The party has proposed allotting £1bn a year towards building the system, though the former army general Richard Barrons told Times Radio the cost of a system similar to Israel’s would be upwards of £100bn.

In a round of interviews at Conservative party conference in Birmingham, Badenoch also admitted her party was “not out of the woods” despite the most unified and optimistic gathering in years. The Tories are still polling below their 2024 election defeat.

“We are feeling chipper because we are going back to first principles,” she told the BBC. “We’re not out of the woods yet.” She added that “people at conference aren’t happy because we’re about to win an election. We’re happy because we know who we are.”

She also said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to form a government, as senior party figures attacked their rightwing rivals with a ferocity that appeared to make the chances of any pact more remote.

In her own conference speech on Wednesday, Badenoch is expected to announce plans to cut – but not abolish – inheritance tax, which is currently levied at 40% on all estates with property worth more than £500,000.

The Tories have promised to cut employers’ national insurance from 15% to 7.5% for people aged 21-24 in an attempt to drive down the youth unemployment rate. Badenoch is expected to say how she will fund the £2.3bn scheme through welfare cuts.

However, she also admitted it could be “difficult” to reverse Labour’s planned changes to the pensions triple lock once they had been brought in, as it emerged her party could head into the next election without a social care plan.

In several interviews, the Tory leader was forced to clarify her party’s “iron dome” defence policy, as she tried to distance herself from using the term. She told Times Radio it was a “semantic argument” and that the new system would protect Britain from increasing threats.
She told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the description had come from newspapers – though the Conservative party press release described the system as “in essence a British Iron Dome”.

In a piece by Badenoch in the Sun, which illustrated its front page with an image of Israel’s Iron Dome, she wrote: “Modelled on Israel’s ‘Iron Dome’, Britannia Shield will invest £10bn over 10 years in the radar, missiles and technology needed to detect these threats and stop them before they reach British soil.”

But Badenoch told Today that was not the aim. “We are not building the Iron Dome. We are doing what other European countries are doing: Greece, Benelux countries – Belgium and the Netherlands – and Germany. We are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here.”

The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, likened the phrase “iron dome” to the vacuum cleaner brand name Hoover when he was asked why Badenoch had denied the Conservatives were proposing an Iron Dome-style system.

blocks.caption: Part of Israel’s Iron Dome air defence system near Jerusalem in 2024. Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Asked on Times Radio if the aim was to be able to intercept any attack over the entire country, Badenoch said: “It should, but it needs to protect critical national infrastructure … Critical national infrastructure protects the entire country. If we lose even one thing, the entire country is in a real problem, and that’s what we mean.”

On Today, asked whether she was ready for an election, Badenoch said she believed polls would improve but admitted the party was still unpopular because of the previous government, even though her personal popularity had improved.

“I think people still associate the Conservative party with the things they didn’t like about the previous government,” she said. “I need to work hard to change that … these things take time. I am the leader and I need to show that this party is different from the party that the people said no to two years ago.
“I am confident that when that election is called, people will see that the Conservative party has the best offer. We have a strong team, we have a plan and we’re all about common sense.”

A Labour source said: “It’s no surprise Kemi Badenoch wants to forget how the Tories hollowed out our armed forces. But hoping her half-baked defence promise based on fantasy numbers will be forgotten just hours after it was made shows how unserious she is about our country’s security. The Tories can never be given responsibility for keeping Britain safe again.”

articles.title: NHL's 'Hot for Hockey' campaign ends after not-so-hot reception
articles.summary: A series of audio stories, released as part of a new NHL marketing campaign and presented like popular hockey romance novels, is no longer available on Spotify after drawing widespread criticism.

image.caption: Asked about the 'Hot for Hockey' campaign during a news conference last week, NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman tied the campaign to an influx of new fans drawn to the sport after watching hit romance-based TV shows, like Heated Rivalry and Off Campus. (Melissa Majchrzak/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A series of audio stories, released as part of a new NHL marketing campaign and presented like popular hockey romance novels, is no longer available on Spotify after drawing widespread criticism.
Series of audio stories presented like hockey romance novels no longer available on Spotify
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 06, 2026 1:21 PM EDT | Last Updated: 8 minutes ago

A series of audio stories promoted by the National Hockey League as a way to tap into the success of hockey romance shows such as Heated Rivalry appears to have been removed from Spotify after they garnered widespread criticism and concern.

The "Hot for Hockey" campaign featured NHL players and games in 60- to 90-second audiobooks, presented in the style of hockey-themed romance novels, according to a Sports Business Journal report announcing the campaign last week.
One of the first instalments, titled "The Storm Between Us," featured Carolina Hurricanes centre Sebastian Aho and the team's season opener against the Florida Panthers on Sept. 29.

items: Heated Rivalry author gets hockey star welcome at N.S. library fundraiser
New cast members announced for Heated Rivalry Season 2

blocks.text: But by Tuesday morning, the audio stories could no longer be found on Spotify.
In an email to CBC News on Monday afternoon, a spokesperson said the NHL had partnered with "real hockey authors, illustrators and voice actors."
"This was a small way to give a playful nod to something that's clearly going on in the cultural zeitgeist — among many different marketing activations," the spokesperson said.
"As a start of the season concept, these were matchup-specific posts designed to run during our opening games in the first week."
The statement did not explicitly say that the stories had been removed from Spotify. The Sports Business Journal had reported that instalments would roll out "throughout the season."
CBC News asked when and why they were apparently taken down, but did not immediately hear back from the league spokesperson on Tuesday.
One of the first 'Hot for Hockey' instalments featured Carolina Hurricanes centre Sebastian Aho. (@nhl/TikTok)
'A joke about women'

Asked about "Hot for Hockey" during a news conference last week, NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman tied the campaign to an influx of new fans drawn to hockey after watching hit romance-based TV shows such as Heated Rivalry and Off Campus, both based on novels.
"And so since it seems to be a cultural phenomenon, we figured why not get on board," Bettman said.
But the audiobooks drew widespread criticism online, with commenters accusing the NHL of appearing to belittle its new supporters, particularly women and members of the 2SLGBTQ+ community.

"I hate the attitude towards women like we aren't real fans; yes I love a hockey romance BUT I have been letting the Pittsburgh Penguins ruin my life for over 20 years and no one will take that fandom from me ever," one TikTok user wrote.

items: What Cornell's alleged rape case and the Hockey Canada trial's striking parallels reveal

blocks.text: Tory Lindberg, a 31-year-old Columbus Blue Jackets fan from Ohio who runs a BookTok account, said she's faced skepticism since she started getting more seriously into hockey after Heated Rivalry.
"I had so many people say, 'Well, you only like hockey because you read hockey romances, or because you watched Heated Rivalry or Off Campus — that's the only reason,'" Lindberg told CBC News.

The "Hot for Hockey" campaign, she said, "felt almost like the NHL was playing into that" effort to make her and others feel like they aren't real fans. "I took it more as like, almost a joke about women and the people that got into the game," she added.

Lindberg also said the series raised concerns around the potential sexual harassment of NHL players by some fans of hockey romance novels. That issue came to the fore in 2023, when Alexander Wennberg, then of the Seattle Kraken, and his wife Felicia spoke out against objectifying online comments they said had gone too far.
"By releasing 'Hot for Hockey,' [the NHL] was blurring the line" between fiction and reality, Lindberg said.

People hold signs during a protest in Edmonton on Sept. 19 against the Oilers' signing of Alex Formenton, one of five players from Canada's 2018 world junior team who was charged and later acquitted of sexual assault. (Amanda May Erickson/The Canadian Press)
Wider concerns
Teresa Fowler, an associate professor at Concordia University of Edmonton, who has written extensively about hockey culture, noted that "Hot for Hockey" came amid a wider reckoning in the NHL.

The league has faced years of criticism over its stance on social issues — from 2SLGBTQ+ rights to racism, to misogyny and sexual assault — and what some experts have described as an atmosphere of "toxic masculinity."
"There's just all this sexual violence that surrounds this sport and … now you want to throw roses on a puck and say come watch hockey?" Fowler told CBC News.
"I think there's better things they can do, like not hire formerly suspended players. That'll get women back," she said. "It's simple."
Hockey fans protest Alex Formenton signing outside Oilers' pre-season opener

Emily Rath, author of Pucking Around and other hockey romance novels, wrote on Threads that she was invited to take part in the campaign but refused, citing its "open mocking of our genre with their 'tongue in cheek' jokes" and "the disgusting use of AI cover renders."
"The NHL knows it has a major image problem because of all the blatant racism, homophobia, and misogyny. They want romance authors to help rehabilitate their image," Rath said.
The NHL spokesperson did not respond to CBC News's questions about the criticism.

Recently, protesters have rallied outside Edmonton Oilers games to denounce the team’s signing of Alex Formenton, one of five players on Canada's 2018 world junior team charged with sexual assault. All five were acquitted last year, and the NHL said they could return to the league.

Longtime Oilers supporter Mary Loewen, known as Mama Stanley, said she could no longer cheer for the team after Formenton's signing. In an Instagram video last month, she urged Edmonton to reverse the decision and called on the NHL to do more to address sexual misconduct.
"This is bigger than one player, one executive and one hockey team. This is about changing a culture that has made too many survivors believe their pain matters less than winning a hockey game."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres
articles.summary: The order affecting two planned data centres follows concerns over forest clearance.

blocks.text: Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres amid concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
The sites form part of Google's record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago and described by the company as its largest single investment in Europe.

The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said work at one site was carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment and ordered measures that would "significantly alter the environment" to be suspended by 23 October.
Google said it had "fallen short of our own high standards in this instance" and would follow the agency's guidance.
The orders relate to preparatory work carried out at the planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani.
According to LVV's head of environment Tommi Muilu, work at the sites included the removal of trees and topsoil, the construction of site roads and storage areas, and changes to ditches.

Tuike Finland, the company behind Google's data centre projects, has been asked to provide an explanation and set out how it intends to proceed by 14 October. The agency said it could begin "enforcement proceedings" if the company failed to comply with its demand.

Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, had previously told the AFP news agency that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been felled. The conservation group had previously called for work to be halted while the environmental requirements were examined.
In a statement to the BBC, Google said: "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance."
It said it had "acted in good faith under the Forestry Act", carried out nature surveys and put measures in place to protect areas of high environmental value.
"As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," the company added.

Google announced last month that it would invest at least €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) in Finland over 2027 and 2028. Its plans included new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, alongside investment in its existing facility in Hamina.
The company said the infrastructure would help it meet growing demand for services including Search, Maps and its AI assistant Gemini.
Google said the construction phase in 2027 and 2028 would support more than 37,000 jobs and contribute an average of €3.6bn a year to Finland's economy.

As part of its expansion, Google also signed a 22-year power purchasing agreement with Finnish energy company Fortum covering up to half the capacity of the Loviisa nuclear power plant. Fortum said the agreement would help support the plant's continued operation until 2050.

Finland has attracted growing interest in data centres, with its cool climate and low-carbon electricity among the factors making it attractive to developers. Lower temperatures can also reduce the energy required to cool facilities filled with computer servers.

articles.summary: The death of an employee at an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk is still being looked into, the authorities said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for Russia to be transparent about its…

image.caption: The woman who died worked at an anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk regionImage: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russiadenied claims that it was imposing anti-plague measures following the death of a laboratory technician of pneumonic plague.
The woman worked at the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region.
The authorities in Russia, however, said the cause of death is yet to be confirmed, and Moscow's health authority Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims the country had put special measures in place.
Authorities deny reports of plague

According to Rospotrebnadzor, the information "does not originate from official sources" and is "untrue," with Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev adding that the inspection had found that the woman's death was a result of pneumonia.
"No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said.
Plague is a disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, known to be the most contagious and potentially fatal if not treated early.
Some reports in Russia suggested the woman could have caught the disease from a broken test tube, while others speculated on a potential link between her death and a lab accident at the institute.
The woman may have come into contact with up to 200 people, all of whom are under quarantine, according to one report.

blocks.text: World Health Organization monitoring situation
The World Health Organization (WHO) said the information it had received from Russia suggests that "no case" of the disease has so far been recorded in Irkutsk.
Russia has launched an epidemiological investigation into a case of pneumonia, labeled as "community acquired," in an employee at the Irkutsk Institute.

"Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens" in the people who came into contact with the person, the WHO said, adding that the agency estimates the risk to be "moderate to low" for Irkutsk.
The WHO is still monitoring the situation closely, it said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is monitoring the situation.
According to Rubio, Russia needs to "share more information with the world."

articles.title: Outcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedom
articles.summary:
Journalists are calling for an urgent amendment to the Special Operations Bill, which boosts police search and seizure powers

Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent…

blocks.text: Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent amendment to a sweeping new bill that boosts police powers of search and seizure, which they argue threatens the country’s much-vaunted freedom of the press.
The government says the Special Operations Bill 2026, passed on 24 September, is designed to tackle alarmingly high crime and murder rates in the Caribbean nation.
The country has spent more than a year in an almost perpetual state of emergency, with police empowered to bypass normal constitutional rights around arrest, detention and search and seizure.
But journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for explicit exemptions in the new legislation to prevent police from searching and seizing their notebooks, phones and laptops.
In the past, journalists have been forced to challenge warrants empowering police to raid their homes and offices.

Although the country prides itself in honouring freedom of speech, ranking 19 out of 180 countries in the 2025 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, this year it fell 13 places to 32, and journalists say they are deeply concerned about whether they can protect whistleblowers and vulnerable sources who share information on the understanding that they will be protected.

The president of the Media Association of Trinidad and Tobago (MATT), Prior Beharry, said the organisation had called for clause 15 of the bill to be urgently amended “to explicitly shield our devices and materials … and confidential source information from standard police seizure”.

Clause 15 prevents police from seizing “a tool of a lawful trade or business” or material protected by legal professional privilege. But MATT says journalism is not explicitly recognised as a protected trade, nor does the bill establish a procedure for handling confidential journalistic material discovered during searches. It wants the clause changed to “expressly name journalism as a protected lawful trade and safeguard journalists’ devices, materials and confidential sources”.

Beharry said the bill’s search‑and‑seizure powers were particularly worrying in a digital era where “the tools of a journalist is … usually [a] cell phone”. Though he said journalists had not been directly threatened under recent states of emergency, he warned that other restrictions were worsening.

“One of the issues we are having is the access to the government, the executive, including the prime minister, who has not had an official press conference for more than a year,” he said. “Ministries use state resources and we are not invited, but state media is invited.”

The independent journalist Pearce Robinson said the combination of surveillance capability, expanded search powers – without explicit protection for journalistic practice – and declining access to government ministers created a “concrete” threat to press freedom, with a particularly significant impact on investigative reporting.

“If your phone, your laptop and your notes can be searched or seized without explicit protection for journalistic material, that raises serious constitutional concerns,” he said. “Investigative journalism depends on people being able to speak confidentially.”

He also raised concerns about phone tapping and surveillance, pointing to an investigation by the Trinidad and Tobago Guardian which said that “judges approved 314 warrants to intercept communications in Trinidad and Tobago between 2020 and May 2026”.
after newsletter promotion
“My concern is not that press freedom has disappeared,” he said. “It is that several of these pressures … are accumulating at the same time.”

Pedro Cárdenas of press freedom and human rights organisation Article 19 expressed concern about the clause in the new bill. “It empowers law enforcement officers to seize any vehicle, article or document deemed likely to be of substantial value. We find this clause particularly problematic because it is vague and opens up to discussion what is substantial value or not,” he said.
He added that it “might directly counter” existing international human rights laws.
The office of the prime minister did not respond to a request for comment.

Stuart Young, Trinidad and Tobago’s former prime minister, branded the bill “unconstitutional and very dangerous”, adding that it “breaches fundamental and entrenched constitutional rights” and was passed “without a required constitutional majority in highly questionable circumstances”.
He warned that the government’s past use of emergency powers — including detaining citizens without charge — showed “the real likelihood of abuse” under the new legislation.

articles.summary:
Kyriakos Mitsotakis said his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, had been supportive of restitution efforts in the past

The Greek prime minister has pledged to “ramp up” his country’s claims to…

blocks.text: The Greek prime minister has pledged to “ramp up” his country’s claims to win back the Parthenon marbles from the British Museum, emphasising that his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, was hugely supportive of restitution efforts before he moved into Downing Street.
Kyriakos Mitsotakis insisted he would raise the issue in the strongest of terms when he met Burnham, who was culture secretary in a previous Labour government.

“Unfortunately they have not progressed,” he told a conference in Athens when asked about talks with London over a muted “hybrid” deal to repatriate the 5th century BCE marbles in return for a treasure trove of other antiquities.

“We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with the British Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.”
Mitsotakis also conceded, for the first time, that negotiations with the British Museum, under the aegis of chair George Osborne, had failed to make headway.

Upping the ante, he suggested the fate of the artworks was also connected to Burnham’s stated desire for the UK to have closer ties with the EU. Sculpted to adorn a monumental frieze that embellished the Parthenon, the carvings have been split between Athens and London since their controversial removal at the behest of Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, more than 200 years ago.

“For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said the Greek leader, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe”.
“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue for Greece. It’s an issue for Europe.”

The combative remarks come amid thinly disguised disdain in Athens for Burnham’s seeming about-turn on the sculptures. In private, Greek officials have voiced dismay that within days of assuming office, he should so publicly reverse his position, stating in one of his first interviews that the dispute was “an issue for the British Museum” to resolve.

Long seen as an advocate of repatriation, Burnham’s support for the antiquities to be returned to Athens dates back 25 years with officials in Athens seeing his elevation as the best hope yet of the row finally ending.

In 2023, as mayor of Greater Manchester, he appeared to go further than ever before, posting on social media: “Send them back, no strings. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”

“His change in stance caused great disappointment,” said one well-placed Greek heritage expert who has legally advised successive governments on the issue. “There was more than an element of perfidious Albion about it.”

The British Museum has been home to around 160 metres of the frieze since 1816, when a bankrupt Elgin was forced to sell the marbles in what, even then, was viewed as a controversial acquisition by the British government.

Mitsotakis, whose centre-right administration has sought to refocus the campaign on the idea of reunifying the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis, insisted Tuesday that changing attitudes in Britain could not be dismissed.

There was, he said, still room for a “win-win” solution with the imminent closure and renovation of the national archaeological museum in Athens allowing gems that had never before seen outside of Greece to be sent to the UK in exchange for the sculptures.

“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”

articles.title: France’s conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests
articles.summary: Prime Minister Lecornu is pledging to improve schools at a time when the government seeks to save billions. France's dilemma can be seen across the EU: How to cut spending when citizens are demanding…

image.caption: Protesters outside the Lycee Sophie Germain in Paris: French students are calling for better conditions in schools as the government seeks to save billionsImage: Eric Baradat/REUTERS

blocks.text: France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is unlikely to have had a quiet weekend. For almost two weeks, students across France have been protesting, angered by class cancellations, overcrowded classrooms and run-down school buildings. The protests have increasingly been overshadowed by serious clashes with police.
At the same time, the government accuses the left-wing party La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting the protests for political purposes and fueling the blockades.
On Friday, Education Minister Edouard Geffray tried to ease tensions by meeting with student representatives. It was unsuccessful.
Instead, a nationwide day of protest took place on Tuesday.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu (left) and Education Minister Edouard Geffray both face increasing pressure as student protests continueImage: Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Sunday evening, the prime minister took charge of the crisis. In a letter to several ministers, Lecornu called for concrete proposals: Class cancellations should be addressed more quickly, school buildings should be upgraded to cope with hotter summers, and the controversial university admissions system "Parcoursup" should become more transparent.

Initial decisions, along with funding and a timetable, are expected to be announced this month. But Macron's ally Lecornu faces one key problem: He has to promise young people more government support while his government is imposing an austerity budget on the entire country.
A signal to the markets

Last Thursday, the government submitted its 2027 budget proposal to parliament. The budget deficit is expected to fall from a projected 5.4 % of economic output this year to 5% in 2027. To make up the shortfall, the government plans to make spending cuts worth billions of euros. France is already subject to an EU excessive deficit procedure and is expected to bring its budget gap back toward the 3% limit set by the European Union.
Student protests in France: Schools shut as unrest grows

"It is an austerity budget," says Eileen Keller of the Franco-German Institute (dfi) in Ludwigsburg. At the same time, the draft is a signal to the financial markets. The government wants to show "that it is taking responsibility" and lay out a path toward reducing the deficit.
No majority in sight for the budget

The government plans to cut spending by the state itself, local and regional authorities, as well as in the social sector. Overall, Paris aims to reduce the budget by around €54 billion ($60.8 billion) compared with previously projected spending plans. Pensions alone are expected to make savings to the tune of around €5.5 billion, and more cuts are also planned in healthcare.

blocks.caption: There is currently no majority in the French parliament for the austerity budgetImage: Isa Harsin/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Whether the budget will actually be passed in its current form is still wide open. Lecornu's government does not have a parliamentary majority and relies on opposition votes. But with presidential elections coming next spring, an austerity budget is even less attractive to the opposition than it would otherwise be.
More money for schools — and more protests

The issue of education in particular shows that France's problem cannot be reduced to the formula "The state is cutting too much." The education budget is set to increase by around €1.2 billion in 2027. At the same time, the government expects around 1.7 million fewer schoolchildren by 2035.

blocks.caption: Many young people are angry about the state of the education systemImage: Nacho Doce/REUTERS

blocks.text: For Keller, this contradiction shows that money is only part of the problem. Public dissatisfaction is linked to what she calls "priorities" and the fundamental direction of the education system, including the transition from school to higher education.
Financing education is getting more costly

The difficult outlook for France is compounded by another factor: the financial markets. For many years, France was used to financing its high levels of debt at relatively low interest rates. But those days are over. The yield on 10-year French government bonds has risen sharply in recent weeks. At times, the spread over German government bonds widened to around 1.5 percentage points, the highest level since the euro debt crisis in the 2010s. The business daily Les Echos ran the headline on Monday that the country was in the "eye of the cyclone."

Market skepticism is hitting France at a particularly difficult time. With debt at around 119% of economic output, France is almost twice as heavily indebted as Germany, whose debt ratio stands at around 64%.
France students demand better schools

Step by step, old government bonds that were issued at very low interest rates are increasingly having to be replaced with new and more expensive debt. The effects of this are clearly visible in the 2027 budget. Estimated around €74 billion, the government will have to spend more on its interest payments than it can afford to spend on schools or defense. According to Finance Minister Roland Lescure, interest payments already consume more than half of the overall budget deficit.
Keller stresses that it is therefore crucial that France continues to be seen by investors as a "credible debtor." These days, however, that credibility depends on more than just economic data.
Markets keeping a close eye on election campaigns

In spring 2027, the French will elect a new president. "The election campaign, which is now gaining intensity, is being watched by the financial markets," Keller says. In an analysis for the dfi, she puts the need for fiscal consolidation at between €75 billion and €160 billion, depending on the calculation.

From the markets' perspective, political consensus on the need for the nation to tighten its belt would be helpful. But, at present, there is no sign of clarity. How the burden will be shared in the future is instead likely to become a central issue in the election campaign.
A French problem with a European dimension

France is an especially acute case. But many other European countries are also currently grappling with fiscal consolidation and how to finance the state. Europe wants to spend more on defense, modernizing its infrastructure and transitioning to renewable energy sources. At the same time, citizens still expect a certain standard of education, pensions and healthcare.

blocks.caption: Student protests are increasingly being overshadowed by violence. The signs are visible at many schools including the Lycee Vauquelin in ParisImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: In France, this conflict can be observed almost in real time. The issue is not only whether the government can respond to the demands of young people, but also whether it can avoid further violence. In Paris, many are wary of the prospect of a new broad-based social movement, like the Yellow Vests protests of the past. For Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, the coming days will be a major test.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Human smuggling conviction upheld in death of Indian family at Manitoba-U.S. border
articles.summary: A U.S. appeals court has upheld the verdict and sentence for one of the men found guilty of human smuggling in a case that led to a family of four from India freezing to death while attempting to…

image.caption: Earlier this year, Harshkumar Patel asked the court to overturn his conviction and sentence after being found guilty by a Minnesota jury in November 2024. (Sherburne County Sheriff)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A U.S. appeals court has upheld the verdict and sentence for one of the men found guilty of human smuggling in a case that led to a family of four from India freezing to death while attempting to cross the Manitoba-U.S. border in 2022.
Arguments 'lack merit,' evidence was sufficient to support guilty verdict: ruling
Earlier this year, Harshkumar Patel asked the court to overturn his conviction and sentence after being found guilty by a Minnesota jury in November 2024.
Patel, an Indian national, was sentenced to just over 10 years in prison after being arrested in Chicago in 2024.
He was found to have co-ordinated the smuggling operation and hired his co-accused, Florida resident Steve Shand, to drive the migrants once they had crossed the border from Manitoba to Minnesota.

In a judgment and opinion posted Monday, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit upheld the lower court's sentencing decision, and found there was sufficient evidence to support the jury's verdict.

items: 2nd man asks court to overturn convictions, sentence in case of family who froze near Manitoba border
Convicted human smuggler wants to self-represent in appeal, questions lawyer's conduct

blocks.text: A panel of three judges found Patel's arguments challenging the district court's guidelines calculations "lack merit," the documents said. The panel said the district court did not make errors in applying sentencing enhancements for creating a substantial risk of death or for the offence resulting in death.
The court said Patel is not entitled to relief for his arguments that the charges against him were "duplicitious and multiplicitous," because he "failed to preserve these issues for appeal."

items: Human smugglers get 10 years, 6½ years for roles in 'unimaginable' deaths of family at Manitoba-U.S. border
U.S. court to hear appeal from man convicted of human smuggling after family froze to death at Manitoba border

blocks.text: It also found Patel's arguments that his convictions on two of the counts were "mutually inconsistent" did not provide a basis for relief.

The frozen bodies of Jagdish Patel, 39, his wife, 37, Vaishali, their daughter, Vihangi,11, and Dharmik, their three-year-old son, were found in a snow-drifted Manitoba field about 12 metres from the U.S. border on Jan. 19, 2022.

A photo posted to Facebook in 2019 shows the Patel family: from left, Jagdish, 39, Dharmik, 3, Vihangi, 11, and Vaishali, 37. They were found frozen to death near the U.S. border in Manitoba on Jan. 19, 2022. (Vaishali Patel/Facebook)

A panel of appeals court judges is scheduled to hear arguments later this month from a lawyer for Shand, who has also asked the appeal court to overturn his conviction and sentence. That court appearance in St. Paul, Minn., is set for Oct. 23.
Court previously heard Harshkumar Patel, who is not related to the Patel family who died, is likely to be deported to India after completing his sentence.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Justin Fiacconi is a journalist with CBC Manitoba, where he has worked since July 2025. A former Joan Donaldson and Peter Gzowski scholar, he has worked in two different investigative units at CBC. He graduated from Carleton University in Ottawa, Ontario, with master's degrees in journalism, and international affairs, specializing in conflict studies. His primary journalistic interest is the intersection between geopolitics and sports. He can be reached at justin.fiacconi@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Russian officials say no cases of plague in city where lab technician died
articles.summary: The World Health Organization says Russian authorities told it that no cases ‌of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who…

image.caption: This undated photo released in 2019 by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, shows the institute workers in a lab. (Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/Handout/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Health·New

The World Health Organization says Russian authorities told it that no cases ‌of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died last week.
Concerns arose after death of 28-year-old woman who worked at Siberia anti-plague lab

The World Health Organization (WHO) says Russian authorities told it that no cases ‌of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died last week.

In a statement to CBC News, the WHO said Russia had informed the agency on Tuesday that the woman's illness appeared to be a "typical acute respiratory viral infection," but that "no case of plague has been recorded in Irkutsk, either in her or in anyone else."

Authorities in Irkutsk previously said the 28-year-old woman, identified in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, leading to speculation she had been infected with pneumonic plague — a virulent form of the bacteria-borne illness.
Shipilova was reported to be a technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East.
The WHO said it had requested further information from Russian authorities about which pneumonia-causing pathogen is believed to have led to the woman's death.

Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian government's public health and consumer watchdog, also said in a statement that no infectious diseases ​had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 days and that extensive testing had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her ​work.
"A comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately organized and implemented in full in accordance with public health ⁠legislation," the watchdog said.

items: Did a Russian lab worker die from pneumonic plague? What we know — and don't know

blocks.text: "This included ⁠identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in ‌contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests."
It said the results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing other infectious diseases had been detected.
"None of the contacts showed any changes in their state of health ⁠associated with infectious disease."
Locals not phased by plague rumours
Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said what she called a "dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed.
She added that 60 per cent of those placed under quarantine as a precaution had already ‌been released. Local media said around 200 people had previously been quarantined.
Locals in the town said their lives had ​barely been disrupted, although they said some people in shops had initially worn surgical face masks as a precaution.
A resident who gave ​her name only as Anna said ⁠the situation was calm and that people had been prepared for restrictions to be introduced, but that life had gone on pretty much as usual.
"Everyone had face masks at home and wore them for no more than 24 hours," she told Reuters.

Denis, another resident, said news of the lab worker's death had been widely discussed in the town and that the local hospital had temporarily stopped doing diagnostic tests but ⁠had since resumed normal business.

A May 2025 satellite image shows the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, Russia, where 28-year-old Darya Shipilova before her death last week. According to Russian officials, Shiplova died from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and causing public health fears on social media. (Google/Airbus/Handout/Reuters)
Kremlin thanks Trump for offer to help
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed appreciation for an offer of help on Monday from Trump, although without making clear if Moscow planned to accept it.
"It's always good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told reporters.
Trump on Monday described the situation as a "big problem for Russia." ​U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information.
Health Canada told CBC News it is also monitoring the situation, though it sees no risk to Canada at this time.

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Canadian actor Simu Liu, star of Marvel's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, has tied the knot, marrying music industry executive Allison Hsu.
Canadian set to reprise role as Shang-Chi in upcoming Avengers: Doomsday
Canadian actor Simu Liu, star of Marvel's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, has tied the knot, marrying music industry executive Allison Hsu, according to reports in U.S. media.
The pair celebrated their nuptials this past weekend in France, according to TMZ, the first to report the marriage, and People magazine.
CBC News has reached out to Liu's representatives for comment.

Officially dating since late 2022, the couple hrevealed their engagement via social media in May 2025, during a trip to Paris. More recently, Hsu shared images from wedding-related events in Mexico and a mid-summer visit to Paris with Liu.
Canadian actor Simu Liu and music industry executive Allison Hsu are seen in a photo from her Instagram account posted in May 2025 announcing their engagement. (Allison Hsu/Instagram)
The couple has been open about their courtship, posting about each other on social media, and Liu has referenced their relationship in interviews.

"I feel challenged and loved and cared for, and I feel championed. I think the best, healthiest relationships are ones where you have each other's back, and I definitely feel like that's the case," he told People magazine in 2023.
Born in China and raised in the Toronto area, Liu is set to revisit his Marvel Universe role as Shang-Chi in the upcoming film Avengers: Doomsday.

Portraying Marvel's Chinese hero Shang-Chi catapulted Liu to international fame, on the heels of homegrown recognition he'd already garnered for the celebrated CBC comedy Kim's Convenience, for which he played Jung Kim, the estranged son of the store-owning family at the centre of the series.
Simu Liu challenges 'out-of-touch' Hollywood decision makers

The superhero turn is among the many projects he's taken on in recent years, including appearing as a memorable Ken in the massive hit Barbie, voice roles like in the animated film In Your Dreams and starring in the spy thriller series The Copenhagen Test.
He harkened back to his theatre roots with a stint in the Tony-winning comedy Oh, Mary! this past spring, which marked Liu's Broadway debut.
