articles.title: Seven arrested for using Ghanaian banknotes to make 'money bouquets'
articles.summary: The arrests are part of the country's efforts to curb the misuse and abuse of the national currency.

blocks.text: Ghanaian authorities have arrested seven people for allegedly using banknotes to make so-called "money bouquets" and decorate cakes.
The Bank of Ghana says the practice is illegal and amounts to misuse and improper handling of the cedi, the national currency.
The arrests, carried out in collaboration with the police, followed a tip-off that led to a swoop on the suspects, all women, accused of selling the bouquets in different parts of the capital, Accra.
The arrests are the biggest enforcement of the law against misusing the currency. In July, the bank issued a notice warning this could amount to an offence.
It warned against "acts that tend to depreciate or impair the national currency, including any conduct that undermines its lawful value or use".
Bouquets of banknotes or cakes decorated with currency are often ordered as gifts for weddings, birthdays, graduations and other celebrations.
The police have launched investigations, and the authorities say the suspects will be prosecuted. They could face a fine or jail term, to be determined by the court.
Dinah Bonzi, an official in the Bank of Ghana's currency department, said anyone aiding or promoting such activities could also be arrested and prosecuted.
''The Ghana cedi is legal tender… and must be treated with respect. The misuse or abuse of the currency is an offence and may attract sanctions under the law,'' she said.
"Today's arrest should serve as a clear warning to the public. Let us all handle the Ghana cedi with dignity."

The central bank has repeatedly warned against activities such as "spraying" - or throwing money at events such as weddings - writing on or altering notes and using them in decorations such as floral-like bouquets in weddings, birthdays and other occasions.
The use of money decorations has become more common in Ghana in recent years, with the practice also gaining a foothold in other African countries.
In recent years authorities in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Botswana have also issued warnings against misusing the national currencies.

articles.title: [Puso at Diwa] When AMLC’s financial intelligence speaks
articles.summary: The appropriate response to AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura's testimony is not to demonize the institution but to examine the numbers

items: The AMLC's testimony before the Senate impeachment court is crucial as it presents financial intelligence that is legally mandated to be analyzed and disclosed, countering claims that it is politically motivated.

The AMLC's findings reveal ₱4.4 billion in covered and suspicious transactions involving Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, raising questions about the legitimacy of these financial activities and their reconciliation with declared income.
The impeachment court must focus on the evidence provided by the AMLC, examining the financial trail and ensuring accountability, rather than dismissing the findings due to political implications.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

There is a temptation in politically charged cases to attack the messenger when the message becomes uncomfortable. That temptation was evident in the reaction to the testimony of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) before the Senate sitting as an impeachment court, with some attempting to portray the AMLC as politically motivated, as though the financial intelligence it presented were merely another partisan accusation against Vice President Sara Duterte.
That misses the institutional character of the AMLC.

blocks.caption: [Puso at Diwa] When AMLC’s financial intelligence speaks

blocks.text: The AMLC is not a political creation of the impeachment prosecution. It is a creature of law. Created under Republic Act No. 9160, the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001, it is the Philippines’ financial intelligence unit, mandated to receive and analyze covered and suspicious transaction reports and to help protect the integrity of the country’s financial system. It is therefore not an optional commentator in this process but part of the country’s financial accountability architecture.
This is why Monday’s testimony is so important, and why the attempt to prevent it from being heard deserves attention.

Before examining what the AMLC found, it is worth considering what almost prevented the country from hearing it. The defense sought to exclude AMLC Secretariat Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura from testifying, invoking the confidentiality provisions of the Anti-Money Laundering Act and questioning the disclosure of financial information in the agency’s possession.

blocks.caption: [Puso at Diwa] When AMLC’s financial intelligence speaks

blocks.text: The objection was significant. If accepted broadly, it could have prevented the country’s financial-intelligence agency from explaining to the constitutional court the very information it is legally mandated to collect and analyze.
The presiding officer, Senator Francis Escudero, rejected the defense position.

His ruling recognized a distinction that should be obvious but is sometimes deliberately blurred: confidentiality is not the same as immunity from lawful inquiry. Section 8-A of the AMLA protects information against unauthorized disclosure, but it cannot reasonably be interpreted to disable the AMLC from performing the investigative and litigation functions that the law itself gives it, or from complying with a lawful and particularized subpoena from the impeachment court. The Senate also recognized that the Bank Secrecy Law itself provides an exception to confidentiality for impeachment proceedings.
This is remarkably consistent with the position earlier advanced by former AMLC executive director Vicente Aquino years ago.

blocks.caption: [Puso at Diwa] When AMLC’s financial intelligence speaks

blocks.text: Aquino argued that Section 8-A’s confidentiality rule is not absolute. The law itself contemplates information exchange, dissemination and access under appropriate circumstances. He specifically maintained that the prohibition does not prevent lawful disclosure to courts and authorized government agencies.

More fundamentally, Aquino reminded us why the AMLC exists in the first place. It was created to gather financial information, analyze suspicious and covered transactions, investigate money laundering and assist courts and partner agencies in proceedings involving the preservation, recovery and forfeiture of assets. Information gathered by the AMLC becomes valuable when it can be properly used by competent authorities.

The convergence between Aquino’s institutional argument and the impeachment court’s ruling is therefore significant. Confidentiality protects financial information from unauthorized disclosure; it cannot become a legal shield that prevents a competent constitutional tribunal from examining financial intelligence through a lawful process.

blocks.caption: BSP senior official hits bank secrecy limits in Sara Duterte subpoenas

blocks.text: The AMLC is not an impeachment prosecutor, a political party or the court itself. It is the institution that possesses financial intelligence relevant to an allegation the impeachment court is constitutionally required to examine. Having been allowed to testify, the more important question now is what that financial intelligence means.
And what it has placed before the court is substantial.

AMLC records presented by Buenaventura showed ₱4.4 billion in covered and suspicious transactions involving Vice President Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, from 2007 to 2025. The records consisted of 666 covered transaction reports and 55 suspicious transaction reports.

blocks.caption: EXPLAINER: What makes a transaction ‘covered’ or ‘suspicious’ under AMLA?

blocks.text: The number is staggering, but precision matters. The ₱4.4 billion should not be described as ₱4.4 billion of personal wealth. It is the aggregate value of reported financial transactions. Money can enter and leave an account without becoming accumulated wealth. Indeed, the AMLC presentation reportedly identified approximately ₱1.63 billion in inflows, ₱1.31 billion in outflows, and about ₱1.46 billion whose direction could not be determined from the summary presented.
That qualification does not diminish the significance of the evidence.

It sharpens the question that the impeachment court now has to answer: What do these transactions represent? Where did the money come from, where did it go, who were the counterparties, what legitimate economic activities explain the movements, and can the financial flows be reconciled with the lawful income, declared assets and known sources of wealth of the persons involved?
That is what financial intelligence is supposed to help establish.

It is also why the characterization of the AMLC as merely a “political” instrument is so misplaced. The transactions did not originate from the AMLC. They originated in the financial system and were reported by covered institutions pursuant to law. The AMLC received, analyzed and organized those reports in accordance with its statutory mandate.

If a bank reports a transaction because the law requires it to do so, the bank does not thereby become political. If several financial institutions submit reports to the country’s legally designated financial-intelligence unit, those institutions do not thereby become political. And when the AMLC analyzes those reports and presents the resulting information pursuant to a lawful subpoena from a constitutional court, that does not make the agency political either.
The appropriate response to the AMLC testimony, therefore, is not to demonize the institution but to examine the numbers.

Aquino’s earlier argument is particularly relevant here. The State certainly has a duty to protect the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts. But the same law declares that the Philippines must not be used as a site for laundering the proceeds of unlawful activities. The AMLC’s institutional purpose lies precisely at that intersection: protecting legitimate financial privacy while helping competent authorities identify transactions that require further scrutiny.
Its credibility should consequently be judged by its legal mandate, the quality of its financial intelligence and the evidence it presents, not by whether its findings are politically convenient.
The impeachment court should also resist two opposite errors.

One would be to conclude that ₱4.4 billion in reported transactions automatically means ₱4.4 billion in unexplained wealth. It does not. The other, equally serious, would be to dismiss the ₱4.4 billion simply because the AMLC has been accused of being political. That would be equally unwarranted.

The proper approach is to follow the financial trail and establish what entered the accounts, what left them, who provided the funds, who received them, what legitimate transactions explain them, and whether the activity is adequately reflected in declared income and assets. The issue is ultimately one of reconciliation: whether the financial picture that emerges can be reconciled with the legitimate sources of income and wealth disclosed by the couple.

The 18-year period is particularly relevant. The court is not looking only at what happened after Duterte became Vice President. Earlier records can establish a financial baseline against which later changes in income, assets and financial activity can be measured. The question is therefore not simply how much wealth the Vice President and her husband accumulated, but how their financial position evolved over time and whether that evolution can be satisfactorily explained. (READ: IN NUMBERS: What impeachment hearings unveiled about Sara Duterte’s wealth)
Ultimately, however, the issue is larger than accounting.

Impeachment is a constitutional mechanism for determining whether a high public official remains worthy of the extraordinary trust vested in public office. The Constitution declares that public office is a public trust and requires public officers to remain accountable to the people and to serve them with responsibility, integrity, loyalty and efficiency.

The AMLC evidence therefore matters beyond banking. If the financial records ultimately demonstrate that the transactions are legitimate and adequately explainable, that should be established clearly. But if substantial portions remain unexplained, inconsistent with declared income, or otherwise raise credible questions about the accumulation of wealth, those questions cannot simply be dismissed by attacking the institution that uncovered the financial trail.

The cumulative picture is what matters: hundreds of covered transaction reports, dozens of suspicious transaction reports, billions of pesos in aggregate financial activity and 18 years of financial history. None of these facts, standing alone, establishes guilt. But taken together, they establish that there is enough financial information to require a serious explanation.
That is not persecution, and it is not automatically politics. It is the essence of accountability.

Perhaps this is the most important lesson from the AMLC testimony. The Philippines should not weaken or discredit its financial-intelligence institutions simply because, on one occasion, their findings become politically inconvenient. The AMLC was created by law to follow the money and help competent authorities understand what the financial system is telling them.
The impeachment court must now do its part: examine the evidence, test the explanations and determine what the financial trail ultimately reveals.

In the end, the issue is not whether the AMLC is political. It is whether the financial intelligence it has lawfully gathered can be explained, and what those explanations, or the absence of them, say about the integrity and fitness of a Vice President seeking to remain in public service. – Rappler.com

Diwa C. Guinigundo is the former deputy governor for monetary policy and other aspects of central banking. He was a former alternate executive director at the IMF in Washington, DC in 2001-2003. He is the author and editor of several books on political economy, regional crisis and cooperation, debt and economic growth and public policy agenda.
He serves as independent director of several corporate and financial institutions with focus on corporate governance, risk oversight and audit.

He also serves as principal advisor for New York-based GlobalSourcePartners. He remains in the advisory board of ASEAN Macroeconomic Research Office and Singapore Management University’s Sim Kee Boon Institute for Financial Economics.
He is the senior pastor of the Fullness of Christ International Ministries in Mandaluyong.

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo, court spox Regie Tongol patch things up after verdict date issue
articles.summary: Senator Raffy Tulfo and impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol have cleared the air after tensions rose when the latter said that the impeachment trial verdict could be out by Dec. 16.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 7:40pm

Senator-Judge Raffy Tulfo and impeachment court spokesperson and lawyer Regie Tongol have cleared the air after tensions rose when the latter said that the verdict in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte could be out by December 16.
In a post on Facebook on Tuesday, Tulfo said that Tongol paid a courtesy visit to his office to clarify his earlier statement regarding the impeachment verdict date.
This came a day after Tulfo asked the Senate impeachment court to admonish its spokesperson for telling the media that the impeachment trial verdict may already be released by December 16.

Tongol had explained that the December 16 schedule he mentioned should not be seen as a deadline for the impeachment court to issue a verdict on the case of the Vice President. He said that date was only based on administrative plotting or logistical projection hinged on the pre-trial order calendar.

“Pinayuhan siya ni Sen. Raffy na maging mas maingat sa mga pahayag sa media sa mga susunod na pagkakataon at ugaliing kumonsulta muna sa mga senator-judges bago maglabas ng anumang opisyal na pahayag, na kanya namang sinang-ayunan,” the caption in Tulfo’s Facebook post read.

(Sen. Raffy advised him to be more cautious with his statements to the media in the future and to make it a habit to consult the senator-judges first before issuing any official statement, to which Tongol agreed.)
In a press conference after the trial on Tuesday, Tongol described his meeting with Tulfo as “very cordial,” saying that he has high respect for all senator-judges, whom he considers as his “bosses.”

“Syempre po [Of course] we recognize their authority, supervision, and control over our actions. Kaya ‘yun lamang po, we just cleared the air and then also, I thanked him for his clarification and his guidance. At ‘yun po, mabilis lamang po at binigyan niya rin po ako ng [It was quick and he gave me] instructions on how to better do things next time,” he said.
“It’s my privilege na ma-Tulfo po [to get Tulfo'd],” Tongol added.
“Ipa-Tulfo” is a famous Filipino phrase which means reporting someone or bringing a complaint to the public service program hosted by Raffy Tulfo. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Argentina to stop Falklands exploiting offshore oilfields, country’s foreign minister says
articles.summary: Pablo Quirno says move is part of government’s strategy to peacefully assert sovereignty over the islands Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that…

blocks.text: Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that his government would stop the Falkland Islands from exploiting its offshore oilfields as part of a strategy to take sovereignty.

During a speech at a thinktank event in the Argentinian capital, Pablo Quirno condemned the British government for failing to open negotiations over the islands and facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.

Among those in the audience was David Cairns, the UK’s ambassador to Argentina. Cairns, who was photographed listening to Quirno, left the event shortly after the foreign minister returned to his seat.

Quirno told the audience at the event organised by the Argentine Council for International Relations that his country’s president, Javier Milei, had a strategy for the “peaceful” assertion of Argentinian sovereignty.

He said: “The British government not only refuses to enter into negotiations to resolve the sovereignty dispute, but is also taking unilateral measures regarding the exploitation of natural resources in the maritime areas that are part of the controversy.
“Preventing the exploitation of our resources from consolidating the British occupation is part of a strategy to recover, through peaceful means, the full exercise of our sovereignty.”

blocks.caption: At the UN general assembly last month, Javier Milei condemned the oil development in the North Falkland Basin as an ‘unlawful act’. Photograph: Heather Khalifa/AP

blocks.text: Last month, Milei told the UN general assembly in New York that the international organisation had failed his country as he condemned the Sea Lion project, an oil development in the North Falkland Basin, as an “unlawful act”.
Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands.

On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline stop the oil project or face arbitration and a binding decision under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS) at the international tribunal for the law of the sea.

The UN does not officially recognise British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.

blocks.caption: Javier Milei and Pablo Quirno at the UN last month. On Monday, Quirno warned third parties not to assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of natural resources. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.

The UK government has said that the islands, known as Las Malvinas in Argentina and which are home to approximately 3,600 people, will remain a British overseas territory for as long as it is the wish of those who live there. In a referendum in 2013, on a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
In a statement issued last week, the Argentinian govenment rejected “the manipulation of the principle of self-determination of peoples that the United Kingdom seeks to impose upon it”.
In his speech on Monday night, Quirno also warned third parties that they should not assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of the natural resources.
A new shipping link is due to be opened between Chile and the Falkland Islands by the end of the year.

Quirno said: “Whoever contributes, directly or indirectly, to the illegitimate exploration or exploitation of resources that belong to all Argentinians will hardly be able to aspire to share in the benefits of our country’s growth.”

articles.title: Australia faces summer of extreme weather, Anthony Albanese warns at pre-Cop
articles.summary: Prime minister tells delegates in Tuvalu and Fiji that ‘super El Niño’ brewing in the Pacific shows climate change is ‘here right now’ Anthony Albanese has warned Australia faces a hazardous summer,…
articles.byline: Adam Morton in Tuvalu and Fiji

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese has warned Australia faces a hazardous summer, likely including floods, cyclones and extreme heat, due to the immediate threat of the climate change and a rising “super El Niño”.

Speaker alongside national leaders at a climate summit in Fiji, the prime minister said the expected nasty summer and the demonstrated impact on Pacific island countries – including low-lying Tuvalu – showed the world could not afford to let the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C “just slip from our grasp”.

“Climate change is not a problem for the future. It is here right now, and we know that sea levels here in the western Pacific are rising at more than twice the global average. We know also that the forecast of super El Niño may test us all,” he said

“In Australia, we are expecting a summer of floods, of cyclones, of extreme heat, and extreme behaviour…The science told us that if we didn’t act to address global emissions this is precisely what would occur, and tragically that is playing out.”

Albanese’s comments came after a delegation of national and global agency leaders visited Tuvalu to see the impact of the climate crisis on one of the countries most at risk. A collection of three reef islands and six atolls, Tuvalu is home to about 10,000 people and mostly less than 2 metres above sea level.

The visit was promised by the Albanese government last year as part of a compromise deal when it missed out on hosting the Cop31 climate conference. Cop31 will be in Turkey next month; Fiji and Tuvalu are hosting a preparatory meeting.
Tuvalu was wet and grey for the visit, and the capital of Funafuti – spectacular from the air on a clear day – was visible only in strips between heavy rain clouds during descent.

After a cultural welcome and a tour of a climate resilience project, leaders held a “sautalaga” meeting – an exchange of views – where they expressed support for the country and urged more rapid action to cut emissions and provide island states with the money needed to adapt.
after newsletter promotion

The delegation heard from Melelusi Sokotia, a 13-year-old local student, who said her friends dreamed of “becoming teachers, doctors, builders” but spent their lives wondering if their island would survive into their adult lives. “We all have one single dream: to grow safely here in Tuvalu,” she said. “We are not asking for peace. We are asking for help and partnership. Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”

Tuvalu’s prime minister, Feleti Teo, stressed island states needed faster access to global climate finance to deal with worsening extreme events. “Why should countries like Tuvalu take on more debt to protect ourselves from a climate crisis we did so little to cause? We should not have to borrow our way out of a crisis.”

The Fijian prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said the world was on the brink of overshooting the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C – agreed in the 2015 Paris agreement – and must bring forward plans to cut emissions. “That is not radical. It is in line with our agreement, our obligation, and the scientific reality,” he said. “The transition away from fossil fuels was agreed to by all of us in Dubai [at the Cop28 summit in 2023]. It is not a new ask, and it is not open for renegotiation.”

Australia has faced criticism at the talks for arguing for greater climate action while continuing to new expanded coal and gas developments. An Australian state regulator last week approved a major coalmine development that would be the largest in New South Wales’ history if it receives federal approval.

Albanese, attending his first UN climate conference as prime minister since his election in 2022, said a message from the Tuvalu trip was that “climate change must be understood as being something more than about science or targets”. “It must be understood that effectively it’s about people,” he said.

The delegation, which include former Australian prime minister Julia Gillard, now the chair of health charity Wellcome, were shown a land reclamation project to extend the atoll by about 20 hectares using sand and gravel dredged from its lagoon.

Tuvalu’s director of climate change, Jamie Ovia, told the visitors sea level rise was projected to increase the annual cost of damage from flooding and storm surges to US$34m a year by 2050 and $63m – more than Tuvalu’s GDP – by 2100.

He said the coastal fishing catch could be reduced by 16% and tuna stocks worth $4m a year could be lost as seas warmed. “We need time to adapt,” Ovia said. “Tuvalu is doing our part. Will you act with Tuvalu and will you act in time?”

articles.title: Nigerian military plane crash kills all 25 on board
articles.summary: Rescue teams searched the crash site after the military aircraft went down in southern Nigeria, with everyone on board now confirmed to have died.

image.caption: The plane involved in the crash is similar to the one in the picture (FILE: August 10, 2026)Image: Steven Mohr/SNS/picture alliance

blocks.text: There were no survivors after a military aircraft crashed in southern Nigeria, authorities said on Monday.
The Nigerian ​Air Force (NAF) announced on Tuesday ​that the death toll was 25, lower than the 32 initially announced ​by ‌Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo on Monday.
"NAF 931 had 25 persons on board, comprising five ‌crew members and 20 passengers," NAF said ‌in ​a statement.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu extended his "deepest condolences" to the deceased's loved ones.
The aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos, Nigeria's economic hub, when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state, Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement.
Wreckage located
Keyamo said the aircraft disappeared from radar at around 9 a.m. local time (7:00 a.m. GMT) and was later found to have crashed about halfway through its journey from Edo state to Lagos.
He said the wreckage had been located near a naval base.
The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42 and said an immediate search and rescue operation had been launched.
A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river as rescuers searched the area by boat.
Locals told AP news agency about what they had heard and seen.
"The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes," one of the locals said.

items: Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial could impact her political future, potentially barring her from the 2028 presidential election if convicted.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Her impeachment trial is far from over, but Vice President Sara Duterte might have already dropped a hint about her family’s future political plan.
In case you do not know yet, the Vice President would be removed from her position and barred from running in the 2028 presidential election if she gets convicted in her ongoing impeachment trial.
So it makes sense that she and her family – if this is really the case – is on future-proofing mode.
But who is the alternative to Sara Duterte if worse comes to worst?

Some think Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte, the Vice President’s younger brother, could be a good option for the Dutertes. He is visible. The Duterte voting base knows him. He recently appeared in the impeachment trial as a witness. But will he run for president?

“Hindi namin napag-usapan ni Mayor Sebastian Duterte ang pagtakbo niya bilang pangulo (Mayor Sebastian Duterte and I have yet to talk about him running for president),” said Duterte during her Davao City press conference on Tuesday, October 6.

Baste inherited Davao City’s top post from the Vice President. He became the mayor in 2022 after his sister ran for and won the vice presidency. Baste originally ran and won as vice mayor in 2025, but took over the mayoralty since their father could not serve due to his International Criminal Court detention in the Hague, Netherlands.

The Vice President, meanwhile, took over City Hall from their patriarch, former president Rodrigo Duterte, and held it for three non-consecutive times. Essentially, only a Duterte has served as Davao City mayor for nearly 40 years.

And this reign might continue in the next years – regardless of the result of Duterte’s impeachment. Apparently, the Vice President’s mother, the always low-key Elizabeth Zimmerman, might have brokered a future set-up between Duterte and Baste.

“Publicly nabanggit ko sa, siguro sa interview o sa speech ko, na nagsabi talaga ‘yong nanay ko na pinapauwi niya ako ng Davao at si Baste na lang daw ang patakbuhin sa national elections…. Sinabi ng nanay ko, sabi niya, ‘Umuwi ka dito sa Davao.’ Tapos sabi niya, ‘Bahala na si Baste diyan sa national’,” said Duterte.

(Publicly, I might have mentioned this in an interview or speech that my mother wants me to return to Davao City and let Baste run for the national elections. My mom said, “Come here in Davao City.” Then she said, “Baste will take care of the national.”)
Article VII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution lists down the requisites for an aspiring president:

items: Natural-born Filipino citizen
Registered voter
At least 40 years old on the day of election
Philippine resident for at least 10 years before the election

blocks.caption: Will Baste run in 2028? Sara Duterte might have an answer for you.

blocks.text: So far, Baste will tick all of these boxes. He is turning 39 and will be 40 years old by May 2028.
But will we see Baste as a presidential bet? It really all depends on her sister’s ongoing impeachment trial.

articles.title: Kenya reports first-ever Ebola death
articles.summary: The patient arrived in Kenya over the weekend from the Democratic Republic of Congo before testing positive for the virus. Health authorities are on high alert and monitoring for more cases.

image.caption: Kenyan health authorities are on alert after the country recorded its first-ever Ebola caseImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kenyan health authorities announced the country's first death from Ebola on Tuesday.
Health Minister Aden Duale said a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo died after returning to Kenya via Uganda over the weekend.
It makes Kenya the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in the DRC in mid-May. Neighboring Uganda has reported 20 cases and France has lodged one.

blocks.caption: Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient died on Monday night after getting sick around a month agoImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the Health Ministry say about the case?

Duale told reporters the deceased patient fell ill about a month ago and had been receiving treatment in the DRC. He then traveled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before taking a flight to Nairobi on October 3.
The patient was suffering "fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites," Duale said.
The man subsequently tested positive for Ebola and died Monday night. He was expected to be buried later on Tuesday in line with public health recommendations.

The health minister said 28 people who came into contact with the patient — including relatives and health workers — had been identified and would be quarantined. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the flight from Uganda were also being traced, he added.
"I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease," he said.
Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew?
What is the status of the outbreak?
Congolese authorities officially declared an Ebola outbreak on May 15, but experts believe the virus may have already been circulating for some time before that point.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded more than 4,000 Ebola deaths out of 8,400 cases since then.

The current Ebola outbreak is the fastest-growing in history, and the WHO has warned it could also become the deadliest because poor health resources and ongoing violence in the DRC have hampered efforts to contain it.
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.

Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.
The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

articles.title: OpenAI delivers a mea culpa to the Australian government in person – but answers still elude
articles.summary: Jason Kwon’s answers were provided in a helpful, quiet and calm manner. For a company under intense scrutiny, there were no missteps Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to…

blocks.text: Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to give the company’s first in-person mea culpa after it admitted – in an unsigned email, to a public departmental inbox – that one of its AI agents had accessed a Services Australia website without authorisation and grabbed data related to Medicare.

Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making.
In other words, just like ChatGPT.
Even the content of his responses evoked the AI assistant he was there to defend.

Asked by Pocock “why did you send an email to an arbitrary department email?” Kwon replied: “In retrospect, we should have done what you’re suggesting”. Asked why Altman wasn’t informed before his meeting with Marles, and why the company didn’t fess up there, Kwon said: “I agree the process by which people became aware of this incident inside our company could have been much better”.
One couldn’t help but be reminded of the way the chatbot responds when pulled up on a mistake: “Good catch. You’re right to push back. My bad, that one’s on me.”

In Kwon’s parlance, the models – built from the ground up by OpenAI, which reportedly wants to value itself at $1.4tn – “accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to.” He tried to explain that the “novelty” of this incident meant the company had “learned our lesson”, which was that it should inform victims of such incidents much earlier, rather than waiting.

Kwon again apologised for the company only sending a casual email to the federal government disclosing that its agent had inappropriately accessed Medicare statistics, but tried to explain to Tuesday’s parliamentary hearing that it was sometimes “difficult” to figure how to make such notifications to a big sprawling public service.
Senator David Pocock helpfully offered: “I assume someone in your government relations team has mobile phone numbers of ministers and various people?”

There was a similar air of post-facto contrition as Kwon – OpenAI’s chief strategy officer – could offer few answers about why the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, didn’t inform the Australian deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, about the incident when they met face-to-face in San Francisco on 1 September. That was nine days before the company emailed Services Australia, and nearly a whole month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.
Kwon said Altman wasn’t aware of the incident before the Marles meeting. After today’s committee hearing, it’s still unclear why.

It’s a big government, and maybe Kwon is right that it’s “difficult” to find the right person to talk to. But some could also argue that your boss shaking hands with Australia’s deputy prime minister would be something of a useful window.
At least, we learned, he said the company didn’t use AI to write the infamous email. Small blessings that they managed to ask a human to write the email – even if it went to an obscure inbox.

But with Australia actually striving to become a tech capital for datacentres and AI – as the revolving door of big tech companies told the inquiry, from Anthropic to Microsoft and Google – then setting the basic rules of the road for these firms, about how they must act and respond to this country and its government, is critical.

Kwon said OpenAI was committed to providing future notifications “very quickly”, and that there were no further incidents they were aware of. But he casually dropped in one staggering fact: OpenAI was still trawling through the activity logs for the agents involved in the Services Australia breach, with those logs totalling 50 petabytes of data.
A petabyte is 1,000 terabytes, or 1 million gigabytes.
Kwon made the mind-boggling claim that it would take a human 66m years – never sleeping, never resting – to go through that data by hand.
The team tasked with checking Services Australia’s email inboxes must be hoping there aren’t any more dramas lurking in there.

articles.title: Fact check: Misleading claims spark plague fears in Russia
articles.summary: The death of a lab worker at a plague research institute in Russia has sparked claims about a lab accident, hundreds of infections and international spread. Some of these viral narratives are…
articles.byline: Monir Ghaedi, Tetyana Klug, Anwar Ashraf

image.caption: The image was published by the Irkutsk institute. However, the institute did not respond to questions about the laboratory’s current biosafety measuresImage: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dozens of people were reportedly placed under observation after a laboratory worker at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and other infectious diseases died of severe pneumonia.

The case quickly became the subject of intense speculation on social media. Posts have ranged from expressions of fear and comparisons with the COVID-19 pandemic to claims about the laboratory incident that have not been substantiated.
DW Fact Check has examined several of the claims circulating online.
Alleged plague lab accident in Irkutsk remains unproven

Claim: "For those who don't get it: in Irkutsk, a lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus and became infected with the disease, dying a few days later," a user posted on X in Russian. "This happened on September 25, and by October 2, she was already dead. In the meantime, she had infected several hundred people." The post, which included a photo of the alleged laboratory worker, garnered over 320,000 views.
DW Fact check: Unproven
There is no independent evidence confirming that a leak of the plague pathogen occurred at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East.

blocks.caption: "A lab technician broke a flask containing the plague virus." The claim has spread widely online, but remains unproven.Image: x.com

blocks.text: On the contrary, Russia's public health authority, Rospotrebnadzor, said that two commissions investigating biosafety procedures at the institute found "no evidence of an accident involving pathogenic microorganisms." The Russian news agency TASS, citing Rospotrebnadzor, also reported that tests on the deceased employee detected no microorganisms linked to her professional activity.

Some social media users have tried to debunk the claim about a broken test tube, pointing to safety standards in high-containment laboratories, where the use of glassware may be restricted or completely banned to reduce the risk of accidents.

The Irkutsk institute does work with highly pathogenic microorganisms, including strains classified in Russia's highest pathogenicity groups, such as Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague.

However, DW could not independently verify the formally designated biosafety level of the institute's laboratories. Biosafety level, or BSL, is an international classification describing the containment measures required when handling dangerous pathogens, with BSL-4 reserved for the most hazardous agents.
DW asked the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute to comment on the alleged incident and its laboratory safety procedures but had received no response by the time of publication.
WHO website update unrelated to the Russian case

Claim: "The WHO appears to have updated its fact sheet on plague the same day the Irkutsk lab worker presented at hospital, with (probably) the plague." This claim appeared in a number of posts on X, each reaching thousands of users.
DW Fact check: Misleading
The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its plague fact sheet on the same day the Russian laboratory worker was hospitalized, but no evidence links the two events.

blocks.caption: Many social media users have linked the WHO’s recent update of its plague fact sheet to the alleged case in IrkutskImage: x.com

blocks.text: According to media reports, the laboratory worker may have been exposed to Yersinia pestis around September 25. Four days later, on September 29, she was hospitalized in Shelekhov with severe respiratory symptoms.

The WHO updated its plague fact sheet on September 29, the same day it published a news release on global trends in cholera, meningitis and plague. The update was part of a broader WHO publication cycle on infectious disease.

The release reported global surveillance data covering 2019 to 2025 and said the findings were published in the latest edition of the Weekly Epidemiological Record, which was released on September 25.
The timing therefore appears coincidental. The previous version of the WHO's plague fact sheet, accessible as an archived page, was dated July 7, 2022.

The social media account sharing the claim also changed its name in October to one that suggests it is reporting live from Irkutsk. Its profile describes itself as providing "sourced updates on the Irkutsk lab leak" and "latest news as it breaks live." However, the account's profile indicates that it was created in May and is based in Australia.
Such accounts can emerge quickly during breaking news events, presenting themselves as local or specialist sources while sharing unverified information.
Old video falsely linked to current plague claims in Russia

Claim: As news of the plague spreads, some old videos are being repurposed, adding to the disinformation. In one such video posted on X, a user claimed that the plague has also spread to other parts of Russia. The caption in Russian reads, "The plague marches across Russia. God has heard our prayers!"

The video is old and unrelated to the current developments in Irkutsk. A reverse image search reveals that the video was initially posted on August 31 this year, claiming that it showed the Russian republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, a tourist destination around 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miiles)from Irkutsk.

blocks.caption: The video shared by users does show a region in Russia where the plague pathogen has been detected, but it is thousands of kilometres from IrkutskImage: x.com

blocks.text: The old video has been viewed more than 1.7 million times on Instagram. The same video was also posted on Telegram. The Russian news agency TASS reported on August 31 that the plague pathogen had been detected in local squirrels and that the area had been closed to tourists.

In the video, a person can be heard saying, "It's at the turnoff from the paved road toward Serebryany Istochnik" in Russian. Serebryany Istochnik, or Silver Spring, is a spring located in the Dzhily-Su area in Kabardino-Balkaria.

The situation in the Irkutsk region is still being investigated, but there are no confirmed reports of a plague outbreak in Russia. Health authorities have introduced precautionary measures following the death of the laboratory worker, while tests are reportedly being carried out.

articles.title: No impeachment trial if VP Sara addressed allegations, provided evidence --Palace
articles.summary: Malacañang on Tuesday said that if Vice President Sara Duterte answered allegations against her "clearly," then perhaps there would be no impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 7:03pm
Malacañang on Tuesday said that if Vice President Sara Duterte answered allegations against her "clearly," then perhaps there would be no impeachment trial.

“Siguro kung magaling siya mag-explain sa mga tinuturo sa kanya, baka hindi na tayo nakarating sa impeachment court, dahil kung mayroon siyang maliwanag sa ebidensya na masabing wala siyang anumang bahid ng kasalanan, wala siguro tayong impeachment na pinag-uusapan ngayon,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said.

(Perhaps if she was good at explaining what was thrown at her, we would not reach the impeachment court, because if she had clear evidence saying that she did not have a trace of sin, we would not be talking about an impeachment now.)

Castro's statement comes hours after Duterte conducted a press conference denying the allegations of dismissed cop and alleged aid of former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco, Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., who accused her of accepting suitcases of cash.
During the presser, Duterte claimed that it was President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s and his administration as those behind the allegations against her.
“Administrasyon. Sino ang nasa likod ng paninira sa akin? Administrasyon. Ang Palasyo, si BBM,” Duterte said in a press briefing.
(The administration. Who is behind the smear campaign against me? The administration. The Palace, BBM.)
“Makikita ninyo naman ‘yung mga declarations, mga statements ng Office of the President, eh. Nandyan pa ‘yung impeachment nila,” she added.
(You can see the declarations, the statements of the Office of the President. There is also the impeachment trial against me.)
Duterte has denied Gracioso's allegations and said that she will submit her affidavit on Thursday.
Castro, meanwhile, says Duterte's camp has yet to provide evidence to counter Gracioso's claims.

“Wala pa talagang binibigay na konkretong ebidensya na na walang natanggap. So ibig sabihin nito, kung may natanggap man sila na pera, hindi ang Pangulo ang nakinabang dito, hindi ang kasalukuyang administrasyon ang nagpasa sa mga pondong hindi umano tinanggap nila,” Castro said.

(There has been no concrete evidence given that they received nothing. So that means if they did receive something, the president did not benefit from this, and it is not the present administration to pass this budget that they supposedly received.)
Asked about Duterte’s comment saying that her brother, Davao Mayor Sebastian Duterte, would run for a national position, Castro said that she should focus on working first.
“Trabaho muna para sa mga kababayan natin ang unahin hindi puro pangangampanya para mai-angat ang mga sarili,” Castro said.
(Work first for the citizens, not campaigning to uplift yourself.)
Duterte’s spokesperson Salvador Panelo Jr. called Castro’s statements “ironic.”
“Sino ba ang walang inatupag kung hindi political persecution at political consolidation? Sino ba ang namamahala sa bagsak nating ekonomiya? ” Panelo said.
(Who has not done anything but political persecution and political consolidation? Who is responsible for the failing of our economy?) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: OSG asks SC to junk petition vs. BSKE postponement
articles.summary: The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) has asked the Supreme Court (SC) to dismiss a petition challenging the postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and deny the…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 7:03pm

The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) has asked the Supreme Court (SC) to dismiss a petition challenging the postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and deny the petitioner's request for preliminary injunctive relief.
In a 64-page comment, the OSG argued that the petition should be dismissed outright for violating the hierarchy of courts.

“The Honorable Court is not a trier of facts. It is a court of last resort and must remain to be so in order for it to satisfactorily perform the functions assigned to it by the fundamental charter and immemorial tradition,” the OSG said.
“...The doctrine of hierarchy of courts demands parties to seek recourse first from lower courts sharing concurrent jurisdiction with a higher court,” it added.
Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal earlier filed a petition seeking a temporary restraining order (TRO) against the postponement of the BSKE, which had been scheduled for November 2026.

Macalintal's challenge does not necessarily question Congress' authority to set the terms of barangay and SK officials. Rather, he argues that Congress cannot use that authority to effectively extend the tenure of incumbents and deprive voters of a scheduled opportunity to elect new officials.
The BSKE has been repeatedly postponed over the past decade. The October 2016 polls were moved to October 2017, while the October 2017 elections were subsequently reset to May 2018.
The May 2020 elections were later postponed to December 2022, but were again moved to October 2023.
In 2025, Congress postponed the December 2025 BSKE to November 2026. The latest law, Republic Act No. 12326, has now moved the 2026 elections to November 2028.

Acting on the Macalintal petition, the High Court has ordered the respondents—the Office of the President, Congress and the Commission on Elections—to submit their comment. They responded through the OSG.
In its comment, the OSG also maintained that Republic Act No. 12326, or the law fixing the terms of barangay and SK officials at five years, is a valid term-fixing law.
It added that Macalintal is not entitled to a TRO or a status quo ante order, saying his allegations failed to establish the necessity of interim relief.

“In the present case, petitioner carries an even heavier burden in proving his entitlement to these injunctive reliefs because he seeks to invalidate a law. As a duly enacted statute, RA 12326 carries the presumption of validity,” the OSG said.

In September, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed RA 12326, postponing the BSKE and moving the next regular elections to the second Monday of November 2028, with succeeding elections to be held every five years thereafter.

The new law also sets the term of office of elected barangay and SK officials at five years. It limits barangay officials to two consecutive terms and SK officials to a single term in the same position. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Cybersecurity at ‘machine speed’: AI accelerates both attacks and defenses
articles.summary: AI can help defenders keep pace with increasingly automated threats but giving machines more autonomy creates security risks of its own as well

blocks.text: AI IN CYBERSECURITY. Both attackers and defenders of digital systems are increasingly deploying AI-powered systems.
Gelo Gonzales/Rappler
AI can help defenders keep pace with increasingly automated threats but giving machines more autonomy creates security risks of its own as well

items: Cybersecurity is evolving as attackers utilize AI for faster exploits, prompting defenders to adopt AI to keep pace, which introduces new risks.
AI systems, particularly agentic AI, are being developed to enhance security operations by quickly analyzing alerts and generating hypotheses, allowing for more efficient responses.
While AI can improve cybersecurity defenses, it also creates vulnerabilities; organizations must carefully manage AI access and permissions to mitigate risks.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Cybersecurity is entering a new cycle: attackers are using artificial intelligence (AI) to move faster, defenders are deploying AI to keep up, and those defensive systems are creating new risks of their own.
That was one of the clearest messages from a summit hosted by US cybersecurity firm Fortinet, where speakers laid out how AI is reshaping both security operations and the systems that protect them.

Society relies on a lot of digital systems. Most of us will rarely see these cybersecurity defenses in action. But even so, it is important that we understand the risks that these digital systems face now, so we can decide for ourselves whether the risks involved with a certain digital platform is acceptable or not for our various uses.

Fortinet security operations strategist Andrew Molly said many organizations still rely heavily on manual triage and investigation, even as security environments generate more alerts, more telemetry, and more complexity. And the problem for cybersecurity teams and systems now, he argued, is no longer simply gathering more data. It is making sense of that data quickly enough.

That means understanding not just individual alerts, but the relationships between logs, systems, behaviors, users, and threat intelligence, and doing so at a pace humans may struggle to sustain. The value of AI, in this context, is its ability to piece information together and help security teams arrive at a judgment faster. This becomes more important as attackers themselves begin operating at “machine speed.”

Cybersecurity news site Dark Reading reported in October that exploitation of some newly disclosed vulnerabilities begin within hours rather than days or weeks, with security researchers pointing to large language models as one factor accelerating vulnerability analysis and exploit development.
Independent security researcher Justin O’Leary, quoted by Dark Reading, described one AI-assisted attack sequence as “nothing exotic, just faster.”
It is this compression of time that changes the balance for defenders.

If an attacker can analyze a vulnerability, understand the surrounding environment, and begin testing attack paths much faster than before, organizations cannot depend entirely on humans manually reviewing alerts and piecing together incidents after the fact.
One possible answer to this? Agentic AI.

In one summit demonstration, an AI system took a security alert and generated several hypotheses about what may have happened. Specialized agents then gathered information to test those possibilities before the system produced a verdict and recommended next steps.
The point was not simply to summarize an alert, but to perform structured investigation.

Traditional security automation is programmed to follow a stricter “if A, then B” route. But agentic AI is being positioned as something more flexible, able to investigate, reason across different sources of information, use tools, and recommend or perform actions based on what it finds.
In theory, that lets defenders move closer to the speed of automated attackers.

But cybersecurity is not likely nor is it ideal to be deployed in a fully autonomous manner, Fortinet argues. More realistically, security operations will probably become a mix of fully automated responses and human-in-the-loop decisions.
Some actions may be safe enough to automate. Others, particularly those that could disrupt critical systems or affect sensitive environments, may still require a human to approve the final step.
But while AI agents may become invaluable for cybersecurity defenses, what’s ironic is that they also create vulnerabilities as well.

The more authority organizations give AI systems, the more access those systems need. And once an AI agent can interact with databases, cloud services, network devices, internal applications, or security tools, that agent itself becomes something that must be secured from threats like malicious prompts and instructions that could allow sensitive data to leak.

Fortinet application, cloud and AI security sales lead Shou Hau Leong raised this directly during the summit by asking whether organizations should treat AI agents as “digital employees.” Human employees are generally not supposed to receive access to every corporate system.

Their permissions should reflect their roles, and the same principle should apply to AI agents, the firm argues. With the recent spate of seemingly automated hacking done by frontier AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic, the term “agentic AI” might strike fear in some.

But as Deven Desai, associate director for law, policy, and ethics at the Machine Learning Center, Georgia Institute of Technology argues in an article, computer systems, including agentic AIs, don’t really “go rogue.”

The AI is merely attempting to complete a goal that a human provided it with, and therefore a human can specify a limit to what it can do. “If you don’t specify the limits of what software is allowed to do, you should not be surprised when the software pursues all possible options to achieve its goal,” she said.
The same applies to AI agents being deployed as part of cybersecurity defenses.

In the AI era, cybersecurity defenses need to deploy systems that can keep up with the AI-enabled attacks threat actors use. But those new systems including AI agents, if not configured properly, can themselves be a vulnerability. The cycle therefore leads back to the human: he or she has to specify what it can do, what it can access, and what it can’t. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sailors missing after fresh attacks on Black Sea vessels, Bulgaria says
articles.summary: It is not clear who is behind the attacks which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea as part of its war against Ukraine.

blocks.text: One merchant ship has sunk and its crew is missing after a drone attack in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.
A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its crew of 18 were rescued.
Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea as part of its war against Ukraine.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn.
Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.
The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said.

A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. It was not clear how many crew members were on board. A search operation has been launched. The vessel's cargo was not immediately known.

Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. The vessel was carrying grain.
Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".
He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."
Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.
A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.

articles.title: 'Ghost particles' from space telescope wins physics Nobel
articles.summary: Belgian physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space.

blocks.text: Belgian physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe.

Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said "his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory".
Halzen first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988.
"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," said Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.
"His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,"
Neutrinos are elusive subatomic particles. The Sun produces vast numbers of them: every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail.
But IceCube is searching for much higher-energy neutrinos, those produced by violent processes far beyond our Solar System — in distant galaxies.
Neutrinos can be thought of as astronomical messengers that point to those fundamental events.
At the observatory, most neutrinos pass straight through the ice, but occasionally one interacts with it, producing particles that give off a telltale flash of light.
These rare signals carry clues to where the neutrinos came from and the extreme conditions that produced them — allowing scientists to investigate places that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see.

items: 10m agoTrump says he will pay for taxpayer-funded ads that sparked backlash for glorifying him

blocks.text: Trump says he will pay for taxpayer-funded ads that sparked backlash for glorifying him
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump has said he will stop using taxpayer funds for television advertisements glorifying himself, which sparked a major backlash, and instead tap his super PAC to cover ads going forward.
In a post on his social media site, Trump defended the ads, which cost at least $1.5m in federal funds and have drawn intense criticism. Trump said they were “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A”.
“This is a rather standard thing to do,” the president wrote, while blaming intense criticism for using taxpayer funds on the ads on the “Radical Left.”
But the president added that he had “decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
Trump provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such future advertising, AP reported.

The White House - which had fiercely defended using taxpayer money on spots meant to promote the president - said on Monday night that MAGA Inc will pay for such ads going forward. It did not answer questions on how it or Trump might prove that his political funds were being used on such future advertising.

The first ad featured clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history,” “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police.”
Later the same week, a second ad began running. It showed scenic videos of Mount Rushmore with quotes and clips from Trump’s 4th July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary.
In other developments:

items: Donald Trump said he was “doing great” as his approval rating sank to a record low 32%. The president made the remarks as he headed to Nebraska, to campaign for a Republican senator there.

Pennsylvania is reporting the largest measles outbreak in the nation, with more than 1,000 cases this year. The governor of neighboring New ⁠York, ⁠Kathy ⁠Hochul, has declared ​a ‌disaster ‌emergency ‌over ​an ⁠ongoing ​measles outbreak there.

Politico was barred from traveling on Air Force One for Trump’s trip to Nebraska, according to a report by CNN. This comes after the administration previously stopped CNN from similarly traveling with the president, despite a federal judge putting a temporary block on Trump’s overall ban on Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House.

Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is joining Fox News as an on-air contributor, according to an announcement from the network. Leavitt, 29, the youngest press secretary in White House history, left the administration after the birth of her second child earlier this year.

The supreme court heard the first arguments of its 2026-27 term, in a case that focuses on whether states can sue oil companies for the impact of climate change on their communities. The lawsuit was filed by local officials in Boulder, Colorado, against Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil.

Secretary of state Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of US bombers from a UK airbase and a suspected Iranian plot at ⁠the site last week. “I wouldn’t just directly tie that to ⁠the move that was made,” Rubio told reporters, when asked about the B1 bombers. “The Department of War is constantly reallocating resources where they need to be,“ Rubio added, noting that the US has confidence in the security of all its bases.
